summary: One of the most yield-damaging leaf diseases of corn. Long, narrow grey lesions kill leaf tissue during grain fill.
symptoms: Small spots with a yellow halo early on
Mature lesions are narrow, rectangular, grey to tan and limited by the leaf veins
Lesions start on lower leaves and move upward
key_sign: Narrow rectangular grey lesions with straight sides that stop at the veins.
favourable_conditions: Warm temperatures with long periods of high humidity or leaf wetness; worse in reduced tillage and corn-after-corn fields.
spread: Survives on infected corn residue; spores are carried by wind and rain splash onto new leaves.

today: Walk the field and check how high up the plant lesions have reached
this_week: If lesions reach the third leaf below the ear before or around tasselling on a susceptible hybrid, consider a foliar fungicide registered for gray leaf spot
Ask your local agriculture officer to confirm the diagnosis; other diseases look similar early on
next_two_weeks: Re-check upper leaves; protect the ear leaf and above, which matter most for yield

chemical: Foliar fungicides containing strobilurin (QoI) and/or triazole (DMI) actives labelled for gray leaf spot, timed around tasselling to early silking
organic: No highly effective organic sprays; rely on resistant hybrids, rotation and residue management
cultural: Rotate away from corn for at least one year
Bury or manage residue where soil conservation allows

prevention: Plant hybrids with good gray leaf spot resistance ratings
Avoid continuous corn in high-risk fields

summary: A rust fungus that forms rusty-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces. Usually minor on resistant hybrids but can hurt sweet corn and susceptible lines.
symptoms: Small, raised, cinnamon-brown pustules scattered on both sides of the leaf
Pustules release powdery rust-coloured spores when rubbed
Heavily infected leaves yellow and die early
key_sign: Raised rusty-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces that leave powder on your finger.
favourable_conditions: Cool to moderate temperatures (about 16-25 °C) with heavy dew or high humidity.
spread: Spores are blown in by wind over long distances each season; spread continues by wind and splashing.

today: Estimate how many leaves carry pustules, especially the ear leaf and above
this_week: On susceptible hybrids or sweet corn with rust building before tasselling, apply a fungicide registered for rust
next_two_weeks: Monitor new leaves; hot, dry weather usually slows the disease

chemical: Triazole (DMI) or strobilurin (QoI) fungicides labelled for common rust
organic: Sulfur offers limited protection; resistant hybrids are the main organic tool
cultural: Plant early so the crop matures before rust builds up

prevention: Scout weekly from knee-high stage in cool, humid seasons

summary: A fungus that produces long cigar-shaped lesions. Early, heavy infection before grain fill can cause major yield loss.
symptoms: Long (about 2-15 cm) elliptical, cigar-shaped grey-green to tan lesions
Lesions not limited by leaf veins; may merge and blight whole leaves
Dark spore masses on lesions in humid weather
key_sign: Long cigar-shaped lesions that cross the leaf veins.
favourable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (about 18-27 °C) with long dew periods or frequent rain.
spread: Survives on corn residue; spores carried by wind and rain splash.

today: Check whether lesions have reached the ear leaf
this_week: If lesions are on the third leaf below the ear or higher around tasselling on a susceptible hybrid, consider a registered foliar fungicide
Record affected fields for next season's hybrid choice
next_two_weeks: Re-scout upper leaves; disease after the dough stage has less effect on yield

chemical: Strobilurin (QoI) and/or triazole (DMI) fungicides labelled for northern corn leaf blight
organic: Resistant hybrids, rotation and residue management are the main organic tools

prevention: Plant hybrids with Ht genes or good partial resistance
Avoid continuous corn where the disease was severe
